lignes.texte: If you think inflation, political hatred, and market chaos are just bad luck in a
temporary news cycle… You’re being lied to.
What you’re witnessing today isn’t some random “rough patch.” It’s the end of a frightening,
historical 80 year old cycle that has governed human civilization and society for centuries.
And every time it ends, the system doesn’t just bend… It breaks.
The only question is what happens to you when it does.
For the first time in recorded history, the United States government is over $40 trillion in debt. It
spends over $1 trillion every single year just to cover the interest on that debt. That’s more than
the U.S. allocates to its entire defense budget. For decades, Washington had the ultimate money
glitch: borrowing recklessly year after year to fund infrastructure, stimulate the economy,
and fake stability. Administration after administration kicked the can down the road,
convinced it would never come back to bite them. Leaders from both sides of
the aisle aggressively spent tomorrow’s money just to survive yesterday’s crisis.
Now, they’ve run out of road. When national debt interest
payments surpass defense expenditure, a nation - even one as powerful as the US - is no longer
“projecting power” outward. It’s no longer an anchor of the global economy. Instead,
it’s forced to look inward, taking drastic actions just to satisfy its creditors.
But servicing the debt isn’t even the worst part. The worst part is refinancing it.
In 2026, a wall of debt is slamming into the U.S. economy.
$4.1 trillion to be exact. Trying to roll over that amount
in a single 12-month period is like trying to refinance the combined annual budgets of
multiple G7 nations all at once. It’s an economic impossibility.
When this debt was issued, interest rates were pinned at near zero. But as it comes due in 2026,
the debt can’t be refinanced at 0%. Instead, it has to be refinanced
at much higher rates. That’s because the US government doesn’t have $4.1 trillion sitting
around in a vault somewhere that it can go and use to pay back its bondholders. So,
in order to get that money, it has to issue fresh debt, at high rates, in order to pay off the old.
That leads to a dangerous spiral. Every fresh “rollover moment” results
in higher interest payments, which leads to more borrowing, which leads
to even higher interest payments and so on. While Washington is suffocating under its own
debt, a separate yet deeply connected crisis is unfolding in the commercial real estate market.
A massive $1.26 trillion of commercial property loans is about to expire. This
market used to be the ultimate cash cow for regional banks and financial institutions.
They allowed companies to take out relatively reasonable short-term loans to fund the
purchases of office towers, shopping centers, and commercial hubs. They gambled that the values of
these properties would continue to increase over time, and interest rates would stay near zero
That entire foundation just crumbled. The COVID-19 crisis transformed “remote
work” from a niche concept into a global trend. Successive interest rate spikes caused property
valuations to decrease, with 2026 prices around 15.8% lower than their 2022 peaks.
As a result, regional banks are now holding hundreds of billions
of dollars’ worth of commercial mortgages that can’t be refinanced at today’s rates
without causing crippling capital losses. And if the banks end up absorbing the losses, they
won’t be able to provide any further credit to local companies. When that happens, it goes from
a regional issue to a national one and the entire American economy comes to a sudden, grinding halt.
This isn’t the first time that something like this has happened. In the past,
the Federal Reserve or even the government could step in and take control of the situation.
But that depends on one important element… trust. And trust is at an all-time low.
According to the Edelman Trust Barometer, a global study that tracks public trust across business,
governments, media and NGOs, society has fractured. Their 2026 survey revealed that
approximately 70% of people today actively distrust anyone with differing values,
views, backgrounds, or information sources. This isn’t a case of standard political divide.
It's a large part of the global population not even sharing the same reality with one another.
7 in 10 people believe that government officials, business leaders, and journalists
are openly lying to them. When that happens, the mechanisms that would usually be deployed
to contain a crisis can no longer work. How do you convince a population to
swallow a cure when they’re entirely convinced you’re trying to poison them?
You can’t. And that wasn’t worrying enough,
there’s one last piece of the puzzle that could turn what seems like a temporary crisis into a
full-blown catastrophe: automated trading systems. In 2026, financial markets aren’t really
controlled by human hands. Trades are pre-programmed, months or even years in
advance. They’re automatically carried out by high-frequency algorithmic execution models.
When certain conditions are met, these algorithms activate.
They don’t pause. They don’t hesitate. And they don’t take the time to double-check with buyers
or sellers if they want to proceed with a trade. Instead, they execute their preset actions
in mere milliseconds, draining liquidity out of the system in the blink of an eye.
It turns ordinary market corrections into multibillion or even trillion dollar fire sales.
These digital systems have so much power, they can freeze everyday payment rails in record time. A
distant and abstract Treasury crisis turns into something that impacts every American citizen,
causing supply chains to collapse and credit cards to stop working when you get to the checkout.
And when you add all these factors together, you have all the ingredients for
a perfect storm of civilizational collapse. It looks, on the surface, like an anomaly,
like everything that could go wrong has gone wrong, and humanity can’t catch a break.
But take a step back and look at the bigger picture, you’ll see something very different.
This isn’t an anomaly, and it isn’t as “unprecedented” as it first seems.
While the precise parameters of today’s situation may be unique, this sort of
situation has played out before. Several times in fact,
over the course of human history. But it wasn’t until the late 1990s that historians
Neil Howe and William Strauss spotted the trend. Their “Strauss-Howe generational theory” stated
that American and Western society doesn’t move in a straight line or random ups and downs,
like a rollercoaster. It actually progresses in incredibly predictable
generational cycles, called “saecula.” According to Strauss and Howe, each saeculum
lasts around 80 to 100 years, or around the length of a healthy human life. And it’s broken down
into 4 distinct stages, or “turnings.” The first turning is called the High,
or the Spring. It occurs right after a huge crisis has been resolved,
when the “old order” is left behind and a new baseline is established. At this point, trust
in institutions tends to be extremely high as people look towards a better and brighter future.
Next comes the Awakening, or Summer: a period of renewal and rebellion, where some people
begin to turn against the established order of the “High.” They begin to place more emphasis on their
personal autonomy and freedom of expression. The third turning is the Unraveling, or Fall.
This is when individualism effectively triumphs over institutionalism. Businesses, governments,
and other entities start to be viewed with far less trust and far more skepticism. Society
begins to fragment into factions which begin to compete and oppose one another.
Then there’s the fourth turning: the Crisis, or Winter. This is the point at which everything
comes to a head. The bill comes due for all the cultural, economic, and political debts
of the previous 3 seasons, effectively forcing a “hard reset” for human society.
It might all sound a little too fixed or formulaic, but if you look back over the
course of human history, you can see this cycle playing out over and over again.
Go back 80 years and you’d be at the end of World War II, the greatest global crisis of
all time. Go back another 80 years, and you’d be at the closing stages of the American Civil
War. Another 80 years back takes to the latter stages of the American Revolution.
It isn’t a coincidence. It’s a pattern. And it’s playing out again, as we speak.
We’re not in the Spring, Summer, or Fall anymore. We’re deep into Winter.
The fourth turning, the Crisis, looms before us. The dominoes are lining up,
and all that’s left is for the first one to topple and send the whole world into chaos.
This is the frightening reality of the Strauss-Howe generational theory. It’s
not a conspiracy. It's based on hard data about how human society functions and how
the conditions different generations grow up in shape their attitudes and the world around them.
Humanity’s most recent High began in 1945. The Second World War came to an end,
and the entire global order was subsequently rewritten. The US emerged as the world’s
foremost superpower, holding the vast majority of the globe’s gold reserves and cementing its
status as an industrial powerhouse. During this time, the Western world
enjoyed a period of almost unknown prosperity. The middle class expanded at a record rate.
Low level jobs paid more than enough for people to easily afford their own homes,
start their own families, and enjoy a good life. And they knew there were hefty pension
pots waiting for them in their retirement years. Institutions were highly respected at this stage,
too, as they always are during the High. People almost universally
bought into the unwritten but universally agreed-upon social contract: study well,
work hard and you’ll be rewarded with a good life. We saw a similar High play out around 80 years
prior, when the Civil War ended. Slavery was abolished, and the Industrial Revolution gave
birth to a new era of infrastructure expansion and commercial prosperity.
Highs are often looked back on as the best of times, especially for the generation that
lived through the crises that birthed them. They realize just how bad things can get,
so they appreciate how much calmer and better their lives have become.
But the generation born into this world of prosperity tends to take a different view.
They weren’t around for the hard times. The High is all they’ve ever known. While
it has its benefits, it’s not perfect. People growing up in an era where institutions hold
absolute power and society all seems to conform to the same rules can feel bored or even oppressed by
the systems that govern their lives. So, it’s only a matter of time
until the next turning comes. The High ends, and the Awakening arrives.
Experts generally feel that the latest Awakening came in the mid-1960s. Many
point to the assassination of President John F. Kennedy in November 1963 as the key turning point.
This is when society started to rebel against its institutional overlords.
Bored of conforming to the norms and following the rules, younger generations wanted to express
themselves in new ways and question the system they’d inherited. This shift gave birth to the
likes of the anti-Vietnam War protests, Women’s Liberation and the Civil Rights
Movement. People began to re-evaluate the fundamental pillars of society of the time,
like family structures and organized religion. Awakenings always bring about change.
And this one was no different. Society progressed and evolved
in different ways, but the bonds that hold people together began to fracture.
So the third turning, the Unraveling, arrived. This is the stage at which individualism
trumps institutionalism. It’s when people become more
oriented around themselves and more trusting of those whose values align with their own.
When society becomes more fragmented and “the establishment” is seen with cynicism.
The latest Unraveling is generally seen to have started in the 1980s. During his inaugural address
in 1981, American President Ronald Reagan declared: “government is not the solution
to our problem; government is the problem.” In the years that followed, mass swathes of
the population weaponized his words. People weren’t rebelling against the
government anymore, they were actively distrusting it. Across the country, Americans angrily rejected
national authority, they rallied against foreign wars and expressed their exhaustion
with wage stagnation and falling living standards. But, while the Unraveling is tough for the masses,
it opens up opportunities for entrepreneurs and investors.
Wall Street booms, global supply chains form, and billionaires are made as industry is off-shored
and civic infrastructure is neglected. While society becomes increasingly fractured and
hostile and the media ecosystem fragments, hedge funds and venture capitalists consolidate as much
wealth and power as they possibly can. We saw this all play out over the course
of the 90s and into the 2000s, leading up to the crisis that would bring about the fourth turning:
the 2008 financial crisis, when the US housing bubble finally burst.
Since then, the Western world has been living through the Winter, the end stage of the saeculum.
The seeds of chaos sown during the Spring are now fully-grown, and it’s harvest time.
The structural decay of previous decades is laid bare for all to see.
The frustrations and fears of the Unraveling have magnified and multiplied at record rates.
Because, in order to contain the 2008 crisis, panicked central banks across
the globe decided to print more money with near-zero interest in order to rescue the
banks and Wall Street. All while sacrificing the futures of countless regular people.
That decision resulted in a never-before-seen generational wealth gap. Baby Boomers now
hold around 51.6% of the nation’s wealth, while Millennials and Gen Z combined hold a mere 10.7%.
The young generations who make up the bulk of the modern workforce keep America running for decades
have a tiny fraction of the country’s wealth. And those same young people are being locked
out of the housing market, saddled with huge student debt and extortionate monthly
mortgage or rent payments. Massive chunks of their salaries are being funneled into
taxes to help pay off a national debt they weren’t responsible for creating.
They are being pushed ever closer to the edge of a cliff…
And they’re taking the rest of society with them. This, too, ties into the Strauss-Howe theory.
It doesn’t just divide time into saecula and seasons, it also underlines the very different
roles and emotions of the generations that live through those seasons: the Prophets, the Nomads,
the Heroes, and the Artists. According to the theory,
Boomers are the “Prophet” generation. They were born during the High and came
of age during the Awakening. They led humanity into the Crisis while retaining the values and
principles they were taught in their youth. They also have the material wealth they
accumulated over the years. Gen X are the Nomads.
They were born in the Awakening and came of age during the Unraveling.
They’re more pragmatic and combative than the Boomers, and incredibly independent,
too. They take a practical, hands-on approach to the challenges life throws their way.
Millennials are the “Heroes,” born in the Unraveling and coming of age in the Crisis.
Plagued by anxieties, they walk the line between desperation and resilience as much
of the burden for dealing with and resolving the Crisis is placed upon their shoulders.
Finally, Gen Z are the “Artists,” born during the Crisis itself.
All they’ve ever known is a world of turmoil, where institutions collapse, economies unravel,
and society is split into tribe-like factions. If the Strauss-Howe cycle holds, they’ll be tasked
with rebuilding society and re-establishing new norms when the next reset comes.
And when you break it down like that, it’s easy to see how and why society tends to follow these
cycles and become increasingly divided with each new turning. Each generation is shaped by the
conditions it became accustomed to. So what happens next?
Back in the 1930s, when the last Winter ravaged the Western World, the US didn’t decide to pay
off its debts through any sort of measured, disciplined monetary policy. Instead, it took
drastic action, executing “Order 6102.” This effectively forced citizens to surrender their
gold holdings in exchange for paper currency. It followed up with the Gold Reserve Act of 1934,
which instantly increased the value of gold and dramatically lowered the value of the US dollar.
A huge portion of debt was wiped out. But regular people were made to foot the bill.
Then the Second World War started, and once America entered the conflict, DC decided to push
public debt to never-before-seen levels in order to fund its military force. The Federal Reserve
placed a strict cap on bond yields, punishing pension funds and investors in order to keep the
national debt from growing too large too fast. Again, the populace paid the price.
Similar scenarios unfolded during previous winters, with the powers-that-be routinely
resorting to currency devaluation in order to control large-scale economic crises.
And that’s exactly what’s likely to happen again here.
Because DC today has 2 options available to it. It could accept that its debts have spiraled
out of control and embrace an explicit sovereign default, essentially admitting
that it will not honor its Treasuries. But that’s not going to happen.
It would be far too dangerous from a geopolitical perspective.
The other option - the only valid option - is to devalue the dollar.
When the $4.1 trillion maturity wall hits, the Federal Reserve won’t have any other option.
They might call it “quantitative easing” or use some other term to cover up what’s
actually happening. But the result will be the same: new currency will be created to
purchase the bonds that capital markets simply aren’t interested in buying at reasonable rates.
And when central banks print money just to control their debt, they don’t really get rid of it. They
just transform one crisis into another… a solvency currency becomes a currency crisis.
The government wins, because it gets to pay off its multi-trillion dollar obligations
more cheaply. Boomers win, too, because even if their paper holdings diminish in value,
all of their real estate and equity portfolios become more valuable. For Millennials and Gen Z,
however, currency devaluation is a catastrophe, the likes of which they have never known.
It wipes out what little purchasing power they have, slams the doors of property
ownership in their faces and throws away the key. It forces them to absorb a cost
of living crisis that is only going to get worse, the longer it lasts.
And what will make this Winter worse than any that has come before are those automated
algorithms we mentioned earlier on. Humanity has handed the reins of its economy over to automated
algorithms and AI models. So when the collapse inevitably comes, it won’t be slow and steady.
It’ll be brutal and immediate. And that collapse is coming.
The trap hasn’t just been set, it’s already slamming shut in real-time around us. The old
rules and conventions that governed the Spring and Summer have been eroded. The current system
is hurtling towards a violent hard reset. The question is no longer one of “Will this
actually happen?” but “When will it happen and how much will regular citizens lose when it does?”
Because history has proven that the Strauss-Howe cycle is grounded in reality. The fourth
turnings may last several decades, but do, eventually, come to devastating conclusions.
History proves that spring always follows winter and that prosperity always returns.
But first, we have to survive the crash. So what happens when that brutal fourth turning
lands? Watch “What If The US Economy CRASHES” to see how it will affect you. Or click on this.
